queries = [
    "LZ dark matter WIMP results 2026 exclusion limits",
    "XENONnT results 2025 2026 WIMP search",
    "axion dark matter search ADMX 2025 2026 results",
    "sterile neutrino dark matter 3.5 keV line status 2025",
    "primordial black hole dark matter constraints 2025 microlensing",
    "MOND modified gravity dark matter status 2025 wide binaries",
    "fuzzy dark matter ultralight axion constraints 2025",
    "self-interacting dark matter simulations 2025 evidence",
]
res = await asyncio.gather(*[web_search({"query": q}) for q in queries])
for q, r in zip(queries, res):
    print("=====", q)
    for item in r[:4]:
        if item.get("type")=="error":
            print(item); continue
        print("-", item.get("title"), "|", item.get("url"), "|", (item.get("page_age") or "")[:20])
        print("  ", (item.get("content") or "")[:700].replace("\n"," "))

content.text:
**Caveat on sourcing:** my live-search budget was exhausted after eight queries, so coverage of literature from 2026 is patchier than of 2024–2025. Claims I could not re-verify are flagged as background knowledge, with identifying detail so you can check them.

---

## 0. Framing: two separate questions

The evidence that *something* behaves like cold, collisionless, gravitating matter is far stronger than the evidence for any particular identity for it. Programmes below are therefore not all rivals: axions, hidden-sector particles and sterile neutrinos are all candidate *fillings* for the cold-dark-matter slot, self-interacting dark matter modifies that slot's properties, and only modified gravity and (partly) primordial black holes attack the framework itself.

---

## 1. Cold collisionless dark matter as a macroscopic framework (ΛCDM)

Support is multi-probe and mutually independent: CMB acoustic peak ratios requiring a non-baryonic component roughly five times the baryon density (Planck Collaboration, "Planck 2018 results VI: cosmological parameters", *A&A* 641, A6, 2020); baryon acoustic oscillations and growth-of-structure measurements from DESI; the Lyman-α forest; cluster weak lensing; and the mass–light separation in merging clusters (Clowe et al., "A Direct Empirical Proof of the Existence of Dark Matter", *ApJL* 648, L109, 2006). These are background knowledge, not re-verified here. Novel predictions were made in advance and confirmed — most notably the peak structure of the CMB and the amplitude of matter clustering. Open problems are on sub-galactic scales (core–cusp, rotation-curve diversity, satellite planes) and in cosmological tensions (S₈, H₀), not in the core claim.

**Verdict: solid**
**Principal problem (if fragile or worse):** none.

## 2. Weak-scale thermal relics (WIMPs)

This is the best-instrumented and most decisively *negative* programme. The XENON Collaboration reported no significant excess in a 3.1 tonne-year exposure ("WIMP Dark Matter Search Using a 3.1 Tonne-Year Exposure of the XENONnT Experiment", *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 135, 221003, 2025), with a spin-independent limit of about 1.7 × 10⁻⁴⁷ cm² near 30 GeV reported at ICRC 2025 — a factor ~1.8 better than its first campaign. LZ's 280-day exposure set world-leading limits (published *Phys. Rev. Lett.*, 2025; announced August 2024), and in December 2025 LZ reported further tightening, excluding WIMPs in the 3–9 GeV range while simultaneously making its first detection of solar neutrinos (LZ Collaboration; reported via phys.org, 15 December 2025). PandaX-4T's 1.54 tonne-year result (*Phys. Rev. Lett.* 134, 011805, 2025) is an independent third confirmation from a different country and laboratory.

That neutrino detection is the key structural fact: experiments have reached the coherent neutrino scattering background — the "neutrino fog" (O'Hare, *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 127, 251802, 2021) — so future gains will be slow and expensive. Meanwhile the original motivating prediction (a ~10²–10³ GeV relic with roughly weak-scale couplings, tied to supersymmetry) is dead across most of its natural range, and the LHC has found no accompanying superpartners. The programme's response has largely been *post hoc*: migrate to sub-GeV masses, inelastic or spin-dependent couplings, and non-standard halo assumptions. Institutional breadth (US, Europe, China, Australia, Japan) and methodological quality are exemplary; the hypothesis itself is not in good health.

**Verdict: fragile**
**Principal problem:** the motivated parameter space is excluded, sustained only by after-the-fact model extensions, with sensitivity now limited by an irreducible neutrino background.

## 3. QCD axions and axion-like particles

The strongest independent-motivation case in the field: the axion was invented to solve the strong-CP problem, not the dark-matter problem, and misalignment production naturally yields the right abundance over a wide mass range. ADMX has now reached extended-KSVZ sensitivity between 1.10 and 1.31 GHz ("Search for Axion Dark Matter from 1.1 to 1.3 GHz with ADMX", *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 135, 191001, 2025), building on earlier ADMX results (*PRL* 124, 101303, 2020; *PRL* 127, 261803, 2021). Crucially, the effort is now genuinely distributed: the Grenoble Axion Haloscope (GrAHal), the Korean CAPP programme using high-temperature superconducting magnets, and interferometric approaches such as ADBC (Pandey, Hall & Evans, *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 133, 111003, 2024) probe the same physics with different systematics. No positive signal, but only a thin slice of the μeV–meV range has been covered, so nulls are uninformative rather than damaging. The honest weakness: the theory does not predict the mass, so the programme cannot be cornered, and claimed astrophysical hints (stellar cooling anomalies, gamma-ray transparency) remain weak and contested.

**Verdict: defensible with reservations**
**Principal problem:** none.

## 4. Hidden-sector / sub-GeV dark matter (dark photons, freeze-in, light mediators)

The natural successor to WIMPs and where much of the experimental talent has moved: low-threshold solid-state detectors (SuperCDMS, CRESST-III — *Phys. Rev. D* 100, 102002, 2019; DarkSide-50, *Phys. Rev. D* 107, 063001, 2023; skipper-CCD experiments SENSEI and DAMIC-M) plus accelerator missing-momentum and beam-dump searches (LDMX, NA64, Belle II). Its virtue over the WIMP programme is that it has *sharp, pre-registered* targets — the freeze-in and thermal-relic curves for dark photon-mediated models — which detectors are only now beginning to reach. Coherent with the rest of physics (hidden sectors are generic in gauge theory), many independent groups, but no positive evidence and a very large unexplored space. Note this is a *class* of models rather than one prediction, which limits how much a null result costs it.

**Verdict: defensible with reservations**
**Principal problem:** none, though the model space is wide enough to be hard to falsify.

## 5. Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM)

Active and increasingly quantitative. Current work favours a velocity-dependent cross-section producing cores in halos above ~10¹¹ M☉ and gravothermal core collapse in a growing fraction of smaller halos (Nadler, Kong, Yang & Yu, "SIDM Concerto", *ApJ*, 2025; Nadler et al., "COZMIC III", *ApJ* 986, 129, 2025), and simulations now include the angular dependence of scattering to predict dark matter–galaxy offsets in merging clusters (Arido et al., *A&A* 694, A297, 2025). New observational channels are being proposed, e.g. massive black hole mergers observable by LISA (arXiv:2511.13220, 2025). The problem is degeneracy: the same central-density diversity can be produced by baryonic feedback, and the objection that cores are not cleanly diagnostic of self-interaction is longstanding (Kuzio de Naray et al., *ApJL* 710, L161, 2010). Much of the model's structure was fitted to observations already in hand.

**Verdict: inconclusive-by-balance**
**Principal problem:** astrophysical signatures are degenerate with baryonic feedback; parameters tuned after the fact.

## 6. Ultralight / fuzzy dark matter

Attractive because a de Broglie wavelength of kiloparsec scale would explain dwarf-galaxy cores. But the constraint programme has closed the interesting range: Lyman-α forest bounds (Rogers & Peiris, *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 126, 071302, 2021), strong-lensing substructure (Powell et al., *MNRAS* 524, L84, 2023), and now cluster number counts from the eROSITA all-sky survey limiting even a *fractional* ultralight component (*A&A*, December 2025, aa54045-25), with further 2026 Lyman-α work on pure and mixed models (arXiv:2606.06969). Push the mass high enough to satisfy these and the model is observationally indistinguishable from CDM — it stops solving the problem it was introduced for. Some room remains via halo-to-halo core diversity in the constraint modelling (Wardana et al., 2026, arXiv:2603.07175). Still productive; the productivity is mostly in ruling itself out.

**Verdict: fragile**
**Principal problem:** the mass range that motivated the model is excluded; survivors behave like plain CDM.

## 7. Primordial black holes

Elegant in requiring no new particle, but the allowed abundance has been squeezed from many directions — microlensing of the Magellanic Clouds and Galactic bulge (EROS-2, OGLE, Subaru HSC), LIGO/Virgo merger rates, and CMB spectral distortions from accretion, as compiled in "Primordial black holes as dark matter candidates: multi-frequency constraints from cosmic radiation backgrounds" (*A&A*, 2025). Systematics in the microlensing bounds are being taken seriously rather than glossed over (Green, *JCAP* 04, 023, 2025), and new probes keep appearing: X-ray pulsar microlensing (Tamta, Raj & Sharma, 2025) and photon-ring microlensing with EHT-class interferometers (arXiv:2512.20037, 2025). Only the asteroid-mass window (~10⁻¹⁶–10⁻¹¹ M☉) can still hold all of the dark matter, and filling it needs a tuned spike in the primordial power spectrum with no independent motivation. The field also has a poor record on post-hoc enthusiasm — the ~30 M☉ interpretation after GW150914 has since been excluded.

**Verdict: fragile**
**Principal problem:** nearly all mass windows closed; the surviving one requires a tuned primordial spectrum and is barely testable.

## 8. keV sterile neutrinos / warm dark matter

Theoretically appealing because the νMSM would address neutrino masses, the baryon asymmetry and dark matter together (Asaka & Shaposhnikov, 2005). But its one observational hook, the 3.5 keV X-ray line (Bulbul et al.; Boyarsky et al., 2014), has not survived: alternative atomic explanations (Jeltema & Profumo on potassium/chlorine), non-detections in Draco with XMM-Newton, and the Hitomi null result on Perseus. Structure-formation bounds push the mass up while X-ray bounds push mixing down, squeezing the resonant-production window from both sides; arguments in its favour, such as the reionization-based case (Rudakovskyi & Iakubovskyi, *MNRAS* 483, 4080, 2019), are now dated. Comparatively few groups, and no dedicated flagship instrument — it rides along on general-purpose X-ray missions.

**Verdict: fragile**
**Principal problem:** its signature claim evaporated under independent scrutiny; the viable window is narrow and shrinking with little dedicated effort.

## 9. Modified gravity (MOND and relativistic extensions)

The programme with the best record of *confirmed novel prediction* on galaxy scales — Milgrom's 1983 acceleration scale predicted the baryonic Tully–Fisher relation and low-surface-brightness rotation curve shapes before the data existed (reviewed by Famaey & McGaugh, *Living Reviews in Relativity*, 2012; Banik & Zhao, *Symmetry*, 2022). And the current frontier is a genuinely clean test: wide binaries at >7 kAU separation, where dark matter cannot act. Here the literature is openly contradictory. Chae reports confirmation of a MOND-type anomaly at low acceleration and attributes a null result by Cookson et al. (2026) largely to small-number statistics, that sample containing only 61 binaries in the MOND regime (arXiv:2607.14450, July 2026; see also arXiv:2507.13177, 2025), whereas Pittordis & Sutherland found a preference for general relativity over MOND from Gaia (*Open Journal of Astrophysics*, 2023). Against this, the framework-level failures remain: cluster mass discrepancies, the Bullet Cluster offset, the CMB peak structure, and the loss of TeVeS after GW170817 constrained the gravitational-wave speed; covariant successors such as AeST (Skordis & Złośnik, 2021) can fit some cosmology but are not established. Author concentration in the wide-binary claims is a real concern — several key results trace to one or two groups rather than to independent instruments.

**Verdict: fragile**
**Principal problem:** no viable relativistic/cosmological version reproducing CMB and cluster observations; the strongest current test yields conflicting results from a small community.

---

## Ranking, best to worst

1. **Cold collisionless CDM framework** — many independent probes, confirmed advance predictions, no serious framework-level rival that survives the CMB.
2. **Axions/ALPs** — independent motivation, distributed international instrumentation, nulls so far uninformative rather than damaging.
3. **Hidden-sector/light dark matter** — sharp pre-specified targets now being reached, theoretically natural, many groups; young.
4. **SIDM** — productive and quantitative, but its evidence is degenerate with feedback and largely fitted retrospectively.
5. **WIMPs** — superb instruments, decisive negative evidence against the motivated version, now background-limited.
6. **Ultralight/fuzzy** — active but has excluded its own motivating regime.
7. **Primordial black holes** — economical, still open in one window, but that window needs tuning and no prediction has been confirmed.
8. **keV sterile neutrinos** — coherent theory, collapsed signal, thin and quiet effort.
9. **MOND/modified gravity** — real galaxy-scale predictive successes, but cannot be the whole explanation, and its key live test is contested within a small community.

**Strongest:** the cold collisionless CDM framework — it is the only programme whose central claim rests on several mutually independent, high-precision datasets and on predictions made before measurement.

**Weakest:** MOND/modified gravity *as a complete replacement for dark matter* — because parts of it are contradicted by good evidence, which is worse than being merely unsupported, and because its frontier results are concentrated in few hands.

**Worth checking further:** (i) whether independent teams, using independent Gaia data reductions, can settle the wide-binary acceleration test — this is a genuinely decisive experiment and it is currently unresolved; (ii) whether XENONnT/LZ/PandaX coherent-neutrino-scattering measurements can be turned into a calibration that lets a real WIMP signal be dug out of the fog; (iii) the asteroid-mass PBH window via X-ray pulsar and photon-ring microlensing.

**Best objection to this verdict:** that I have conflated *programme health* with *evidential support* in a way that flatters ΛCDM and penalises MOND. On the criterion the philosophy of science usually treats as most probative — successful novel prediction — MOND on galaxy scales outperforms every particle programme here, none of which has predicted a confirmed new phenomenon. One can argue that the galaxy-scale regularities MOND predicted are an unexplained brute fact for CDM that feedback models fit only after the event, and that ranking MOND last therefore rewards institutional scale over predictive success. My defence is that failing on clusters and the CMB is a harder failure than lacking an explanation for a scaling relation — but I hold that judgement with moderate confidence, and would hold it more weakly if the wide-binary anomaly is independently confirmed. I am also least confident in the relative placement of SIDM versus WIMPs, which turns on how much credit a programme gets for excellent instrumentation aimed at a hypothesis that has largely failed.
